subject: ENG
label: Grade 11 Commerce
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 11 Commerce English, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 5 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.

modules.title: Prose and poetry from world writers
modules.outcome: analyse theme and voice in two texts
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Prose and poetry from world writers', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: analyse theme and voice in two texts. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Prose and poetry from world writers' twice. You repeat them aloud.
Notice the pattern: find where the new sound, word form or sentence rule appears in a short text and mark it.
Use it: analyse theme and voice in two texts, first with help, then alone.
Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Simile: 'The moon is like a silver coin.' Metaphor: 'The classroom was a zoo.' Imagery: 'the dew-wet grass' appeals to sight and touch. Say what feeling each creates. Method: Model run for 'Prose and poetry from world writers'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Analyse theme and voice in two texts: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Read Text A, a prose extract. 'Every dawn Salma counted the coins in the cash tin, though she knew the number. Her father had taught her that a trader who stops counting stops caring. By noon the tin was heavy, but her shoulders were heavier.' Note the narrator's close, third-person voice.

Step 2, Read Text B, a poem. 'The ledger has no column for the hours, / no line for the aching back. / It records what was sold and what was owed, / and the rest goes under black.' Notice the speaker is quiet and critical. Both texts concern work, money and what the numbers leave out.

Step 3, Identify the theme in each. Text A: honest daily work carries an unseen physical and emotional cost. Text B: accounts record money but ignore human effort. Shared theme: the human cost behind commercial figures. State each in one clear sentence and avoid retelling the story.

Step 4, Analyse voice. In Text A the calm narrator uses routine verbs ('counted', 'taught') and a balanced last line ('heavy' against 'heavier'), a tone of respectful sympathy. In Text B the speaker uses an accounting metaphor and a blunt rhyme (back, black), a tone of quiet protest.

Step 5, Write a comparison. 'Both texts reveal the hidden cost of work. In Text A the narrator quietly describes Salma's "heavier" shoulders, while in Text B the speaker protests that the ledger has "no line for the aching back". The first sympathises; the second criticises.' Use short quotations.

Step 6, Your turn: what does 'goes under black' suggest in Text B? Model answer: It suggests that unrecorded effort is hidden or erased, like a line struck out in dark ink, and it repeats the poem's idea that business records ignore human suffering.

modules.title: Grammar and editing
modules.outcome: edit text for tense, agreement and clarity
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'Grammar and editing', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: edit text for tense, agreement and clarity. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Listen first: your teacher or a recording says the new words or sentences from 'Grammar and editing' twice. You repeat them aloud.

Check and fix: read your work aloud once more; fix one thing you hear is wrong.
modules.example: Solved: Passive: 'The cat chased the mouse' becomes 'The mouse was chased by the cat.' Reported: 'I will come,' she said becomes She said that she would come. Modals: 'should' for advice, 'must' for rules. Agreement: 'The list of items is long.' Edit: 'He go to school' becomes 'He goes to school.' Method: Model run for 'Grammar and editing'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Edit text for tense, agreement and clarity: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Edit for tense. Passage: 'Last quarter the company launches a new product and sold 500 units.' The time marker 'last quarter' demands the past tense, so the corrected version is 'launched a new product and sold 500 units'. Underline the time clue first, then check each verb against it.

Step 2, Edit for agreement. 'The list of suppliers are updated every month.' The subject is 'list', singular, so write 'is updated'. 'Each of the clerks have a desk' becomes 'has'. 'Neither the manager nor the clerks was present' becomes 'were present', matching the nearer plural subject.

Step 3, Edit for clarity. 'Walking into the office, the printer was broken.' The printer did not walk. Rewrite: 'Walking into the office, I found the printer broken.' A modifier must sit next to the word it describes. Another: 'We discussed the report with the clients that was late' becomes 'the late report'.

Step 4, Remove wordiness. 'Due to the fact that the sales declined, we are in a position to say that profit was lower' becomes 'Because sales declined, profit was lower.' Cut empty phrases, keep the key fact and the verb. This improves clarity without losing meaning.

Step 5, Edit a whole passage. Original: 'The firm have grown fast, and their managers works long hours, so it is hoped that results was good.' Edited: 'The firm has grown fast, and its managers work long hours, so results are expected to be good.' Check tense, agreement, pronoun and clarity.

Step 6, Your turn: correct 'The number of customers have increased since the new shop open.' Answer: 'The number of customers has increased since the new shop opened.' 'Number' is singular, so use 'has', and the past time clause needs 'opened'.

modules.example: Solved: Formal letter: 12 November 2026; The Principal; Subject: request for a library card; 'Respected Sir, I am a student of Class 8...'; Yours faithfully, Aman. Informal: Dear Ria, ... Your friend, Aman. Report: title, date, place, what happened, result, writer's name. Method: Model run for 'Writing: speeches, articles and reports'. Teacher text (3 lines about a daily activity). Step 1, read it aloud together. Step 2, mark every word or sentence that uses the new pattern. Step 3, a learner writes or says two new lines of their own that use the same pattern. Step 4, the learner reads them aloud and corrects one slip. What a good answer looks like: the pattern is used correctly in both lines, the lines make sense, and the learner can say which part is the pattern.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Write persuasive and informative pieces: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Decide purpose and audience. A persuasive piece, such as a speech, aims to move people; an informative piece, such as a report, explains facts. Example task: persuade shop owners to accept digital payments. Audience: local traders. List two benefits and one worry to answer: safety and speed, against set-up cost.

Step 2, Collect numbers. A survey of 200 customers found that 150 prefer paying digitally: 150 divided by 200 is 75 percent. Sales rose from 80,000 to 92,000 after one shop adopted it: 12,000 divided by 80,000 is 15 percent growth. Persuasion grows stronger with exact figures.

Step 3, Write the speech opening and body. 'Friends and fellow traders, what if three out of four of your customers could pay you in seconds? Three in four, or 75 percent, already prefer digital payment.' Add the sales point: 'One shop grew by 15 percent.' Use a rhetorical question and the rule of three.

Step 4, Close the speech with a call to action. 'Do not wait for your competitors to move first. Try it for one month, and let the numbers decide. Thank you.' Keep sentences short, repeat the key phrase, and end firmly. Pauses and tone matter more in speaking than in writing.

Step 5, Write the informative version as a short report. Title, date, introduction, findings, recommendation. 'Findings: 75 percent of 200 customers prefer digital payment. Sales at the pilot shop rose by 15 percent. Recommendation: extend the pilot to three more shops.' Use neutral third-person and no emotive words.

Step 6, Your turn: a survey of 80 customers found 20 want longer opening hours. Express this as a percentage in a sentence. Answer: 'Of the 80 customers surveyed, 20, or 25 percent, want longer opening hours.' Check: 20 divided by 80 is 0.25.

modules.standard: Answer inference and evaluation questions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Read my own passage once for gist. "The market stall owner lowered her prices every evening, yet her loyal buyers never seemed to notice; they came for her smile, not her bargains." Gist: customers value relationship over discount.

Step 2, Annotate tone and key words. "Lowered", "yet", "never seemed to notice" show a mild irony: the discount fails to change behaviour. Reason: connectives such as "yet" signal contrast, and contrast often carries the inference.

Step 3, Answer an inference question. Question: "Why do buyers return?" Weak: "They like prices." Strong: "They return because they value her friendliness; the phrase 'not her bargains' shows price is not the reason." Reason: cite words and explain.

Step 4, Answer an evaluation question. "How effective is the writer's contrast?" Model: "The contrast between 'bargains' and 'smile' is effective because it makes a business lesson clear in a single, balanced clause."

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "The writer uses a metaphor." (no example, no effect) Right: "The word 'loyal' suggests commitment beyond transaction, so it reinforces the idea of relationship." Name a technique only when you explain its effect.

Step 6, Read a short poem, my own: "The ledger closed. The lamp burned low, / and numbers lost their steady flow." Inference: the day's work is ending and the speaker is tired. Evidence: "lamp burned low" and "lost their steady flow".

Step 7, Your turn. Passage: "After the merger, the office grew quiet; colleagues ate lunch alone." What does this suggest? Model answer: "It suggests that the merger created uncertainty or distance; 'grew quiet' and 'alone' show lost team spirit."

modules.standard: Deliver a structured speech and respond to questions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Plan a structured speech with a thesis. Topic: "Small businesses need digital skills." Thesis: "Digital skills decide whether a small business survives." Structure: hook, thesis, three points, rebuttal, conclusion.

Step 2, Write the hook and thesis. "Last year, a corner shop in my town doubled its sales by selling online. Digital skills are not a luxury for small businesses; they are the difference between growth and closure." Reason: a story plus a claim engages the audience.

Step 3, Develop point one with evidence. "First, customers search before they buy. If a business is not visible online, it loses them before they reach the door." Reason: each point should be one claim plus its reason.

Step 4, Add rebuttal. "Some argue that traditional service matters more. It does, but good service reaches more people when it is combined with online ordering." Reason: a rebuttal shows you consider the other side.

Step 5, Fix an error. Weak: "As I said, digital is good, so, um, it is good." Better: "Therefore, a business that invests in digital skills improves its sales and its resilience." Remove fillers and repetition, and use signposts.

Step 6, Close and handle a question. "In conclusion, digital skills protect and grow small businesses." Q: "Isn't training expensive?" A: "It can be, but the cost of staying invisible is higher; free online courses reduce that cost."

Step 7, Your turn. Write a thesis and a rebuttal sentence for a speech on "Customers deserve transparent pricing". Model answer: "Thesis: Transparent pricing builds trust and repeat sales." "Rebuttal: Some firms fear losing flexibility, but clear base prices still allow fair discounts."
